s13a.slug: THURSDAY · 9:40 AM · DELGADO HALL, THE MAILBOXES — TWO ENVELOPES
body: The mailroom window is a white square this morning. The marine layer has followed him up the hill from the Commons and settled on the jacaranda outside, and the bare twigs are dripping on the sill without its having rained. Under Priya’s laminate, PACKAGE SLIPS ARE NOT NOTES TO SELF, last week’s Sharpie *they are now* has picked up an answer in green ballpoint, *they always were*, and somebody has drawn a fleur-de-lis under that, because this week somebody draws one under everything.
412’s box is in the third row, at the height of his belt, and its little brass door sticks, as it always has; he has to put his thumb on the 4 and lift. There’s more in it than a bookstore circular.

On top is a long white envelope addressed in block capitals that climb a little toward the end of every line, the way they climbed on the back of every birthday card his brother ever signed. The stamp in the corner says what it says.

body.title: Envelope, Ohio postmark, a stamp in the corner: INMATE CORRESPONDENCE
body.text:
MISS SKYE CALLENDER
c/o JACK COSTIGAN
DELGADO HALL
MARISOL, CALIFORNIA

DANIEL F. COSTIGAN A555218

body: *Don’t read it*, Danny said on Tuesday, with a CO saying his name behind him. *And don’t do the face.* The flap has been sealed and then taped over by a CO who has already read it and was careful about it. Jack holds it up to the white window and gets nothing for his trouble but lines of capitals showing through the paper backward, mirror writing he could work out if he stood here long enough, and he isn’t going to stand here. He zips it into the inside pocket of the Carhartt.
Under it is a card.

It’s folded once, cream, of a stock heavy enough to stand up on its own, and there’s a fleur-de-lis at the top — not printed, pressed into the paper, so that his thumb finds it before his eyes do. Marisol doesn’t run to paper like this. Somebody’s mother does. On the outside, in pencil, it says *Jack*, and he knows the hand from the margins of half the books on his shelf: the J that starts above the line, the k with a kick in its leg, a pencil kept sharp enough to cut.
At the far end of the wall, past the 300s, the 200s are in the shade, and there’s nobody at 217. He opens it standing up, with his bag still on his shoulder.

body.title: A cream card, a fleur-de-lis pressed at the top
body.text:
Jack —

Theo says you’re not coming. Mémère says that isn’t a thing people say to her. Mama has made up the twins’ room, and Daddy says the Saints have never won one with a Costigan in the house, which is true.

American, Friday, 1:15. There’s a seat.

You’d be welcome.

—L.

body: Which is true. The Saints have never won one with anybody in the house.

The room is Theo’s. Theo said that on Tuesday in the Anchor’s back booth, in those words, with the mother’s name in front of it like a screen credit. The flight is Theo’s too, to the minute; Jack has seen it on an e-ticket with his own name printed under it. Theo has been at this since Tuesday with a pen and a placemat, and now it has come around again on better paper. Theo’s script in her handwriting, Jack figures. Or her mother’s manners, which would want an invitation sent on the good stock whether anybody meant it or not.

Either way it’s an answer to a question he already answered. He folds it back along its crease and puts it in the *Brideshead* in his back pocket, at Book Three. It’s stiff enough to make a good bookmark. He’ll be able to find his place by feel.

Doug comes in from the lobby in shower shoes, says “Dude,” with some urgency, to the package window, and is handed a box the size of a microwave that says LOGITECH on the side. “Speakers,” he tells Jack, holding it up like a newborn. “For the island. Dude, *surround*.” He goes out hugging it.
Jack shuts 412’s little door. It sticks. He lifts, with his thumb on the 4, and it latches.

s14.slug: THURSDAY · 1:00 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — PHIL 109H — THROUGH THE CHAIR
body: The fog has gone off the hill by one, and the wind that took it is working the eucalyptus outside 302, so that at the window end of the long table the light keeps arriving and leaving. At the door end, under the clock, there’s only the fluorescent tube and the radiator. That end is Jack’s.

It is the first time the table has sat since the door on its trestles. Evan is at the door with the roster on its clipboard, clicking his pen at each name. Yusuf has the corner, his Commons coffee with the lid on it, and a ballpoint beside the cup with its cap on too. The two girls from the window side have their *Brideshead*s out, one of them a library copy in a plastic jacket that crackles whenever she turns a page. Caleb, whose account of last Wednesday went through Delgado by way of Doug and came out the other end with chairs in it, is sitting so still he could be having his portrait taken in 1890.
At the window end, in the last chair, Lena has her copy squared to the edge of the table with the pencil laid across it. It’s a long table. That’s what it’s for.

Hale comes in at four minutes past with his coat over his arm and the Williams in his back pocket. He has shaved, and missed a place under the jaw, and his eyes are pink at the rims. He takes the roster from Evan without reading it and sits down halfway along the side, where he has to turn his head for either end, and he turns it now, to one end and then the other, taking his time about each.

“I have spent four days in New York being called *my dear man* by a bishop on a stage,” he says. “I find I’m in the mood for intermediaries.” He lays the roster down. “Until I say otherwise, Mr. Costigan and Miss Broussard will address all remarks to the chair.”
Caleb’s hand comes partway up off the table. “Is that —” He looks for the word. “Legal?”

“It’s pedagogy, Mr. Hargrove.” Hale gets up, uncaps a marker and writes on the whiteboard behind him in his tilted capitals, IS JULIA RIGHT TO SEND CHARLES AWAY?, and caps the marker and sits back down. “The chair is me. You will find the chair accurate, impartial and very slightly drunk on the sound of its own voice, which is to say a chair like any other. Miss Broussard. The floor. Address it to me.”
Lena leaves the book shut.

“Yes, Professor,” she says, to Hale. “She’s right, and it’s the only honest thing anybody does in the whole novel. Everybody in that house is lying to somebody. Charles is lying to his wife. Rex is lying to everyone, professionally. Bridey isn’t lying, but that’s only because nobody has ever asked him a question. Julia looks straight at the one thing she wants most in the world, says out loud exactly what it’s going to cost her, and pays it.” Now she does open the book, to a page she doesn’t have to look for. “She won’t *set up a rival good to God’s*. She doesn’t dress it up as a sacrifice, either — she calls it a bargain, she’s that honest. Lord have mercy, Professor. A woman who knows the price and pays it anyway isn’t a fanatic. She’s the only grown-up in the book.”

Hale turns his head the long way back, past Caleb’s portrait and Yusuf’s capped pen, to the door end. “Miss Broussard says,” he says, “and I am paraphrasing only slightly: *yes, obviously*.” He folds his hands on the roster. “Mr. Costigan. The chair awaits your reply. The chair is not getting any younger.”

It’s easier than he would have thought. A sentence goes down the table to Hale and comes back with Hale’s fingerprints on it, and none of it has to travel the length of the varnish in a straight line. He has had worse arrangements. He has, this month, had nearly all of them.

choices.text: “Professor, she calls it a private bargain. Tell her Charles pays for it and never signed it.”
response: Hale delivers it down the table with both eyebrows. “Mr. Costigan observes that the bargain is private, and the bill has gone to Mr. Ryder.”

“Then tell Mr. Costigan Charles isn’t paying for her bargain, Professor,” Lena says. “He’s being spared. Spared a woman who’d have hated him inside a year for being the thing she put in God’s place — and hated herself worse, and taken it out on the furniture. She’s doing him a kindness he’s too proud to recognize. Men usually are.”
Hale relays it intact, down to the furniture. Yusuf writes something on his legal pad, reads it back, and crosses it out.

choices.text: “Professor, tell Miss Broussard that Waugh rigs the deck — he hands Julia God and Charles a paintbrush.”
response: “Mr. Costigan,” Hale tells the window end, enjoying himself enormously, “feels the deck is rigged.”
“Tell Mr. Costigan,” Lena says, to Hale, “the paintbrush is the only thing Charles ever loved that didn’t love him back.”
Caleb laughs, and stops, and goes back to sitting for his portrait. It’s a better line than Jack’s. From the door end he can afford to admit that, to himself.

choices.text: “She’s right that it costs Julia. Tell her I’ll give her that.”
response: Hale relays it slowly, with one eyebrow up, and doesn’t improve it.
At the window end there’s a pause, a short one, that Lena doesn’t use for anything. “Tell him thank you,” she says, to Hale.
It’s the only thank-you of the hour, and it goes to the chair. Evan’s pen stops on the roster. “The chair is moved,” Hale says, drily, “and expects to recover.”

choices.text: “Ask her whether Charles was ever asked what he believed.”
response: Hale asks her, turning the top half of himself toward the window to do it.

“He was asked every day for ten years, Professor,” Lena says. “By every Flyte in that house, at every meal, with the chapel right off the hall. Lady Marchmain asked him. Cordelia asked him. Sebastian asked him just by being Sebastian. And every single time he answered with that face he makes, the one like he’s smelled the sacristy.” She doesn’t wait for Hale. “Asking isn’t the trouble in that book. Answering is.”
Hale turns back to the door end. “Mr. Costigan,” he says, “you’ve been answered.” On the window side the girl with the library copy writes *answering is* in her margin and draws a box around it.

s14a.slug: THURSDAY · 1:25 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — A TWITCH UPON THE THREAD
body: Twenty minutes in, the room has learned the rhythm the way a congregation learns a new Mass setting: a line goes down to Hale, Hale turns his head, the line goes on, and every head at the table goes with it, down and back. Yusuf has stopped pretending to read and holds his coffee in both hands, following. Evan has written the date at the top of a fresh page of the roster and nothing under it.
Caleb is the first to crack. “Can *I* talk to her?” he asks Hale. “Like, directly? Is that allowed? For the rest of us?”
“The rule binds the principals, Mr. Hargrove. You may address anybody you like.” Hale doesn’t look round. “I can’t promise anyone will listen. That has always been the case.”

Caleb turns in his chair toward the window end and opens his mouth, and discovers that he has nothing to say to Lena Broussard about *Brideshead Revisited* that he wants to say in this room, today, with Jack Costigan under the clock; and he turns back, and studies the whiteboard as though it might be on the final.
At the window end Lena lifts her pencil off the book.
“Miss Broussard has asked the chair for the floor,” Hale says, “by raising a pencil, which the chair has decided to treat as a motion.”

“It’s the title of the whole last part, Professor,” Lena says. “And Waugh didn’t make it up. He took it from Chesterton. Father Brown says it, at the end of one of the stories — he caught the thief with an unseen hook and an invisible line, long enough to let him wander to the ends of the world, and still bring him back with a twitch upon the thread. Lady Marchmain reads it out loud to the family after dinner, and nobody’s listening, and every one of them gets that twitch before the book’s over. Lord Marchmain gets it on his deathbed, with his hand. Sebastian gets it in Tunis — he ends up at the gate of a monastery carrying the monks’ bags, drunk half the time, and as near to God as anybody in the novel. Julia gets it at the same bedside. Charles gets it last. That isn’t a cage, Professor. A cage doesn’t let you go anywhere. That line lets you go everywhere. It’s just long.”

Hale relays it, and this time he doesn’t trim it: the hook, the line, the ends of the world, Tunis. He finishes on *It’s just long* in her cadence and not his, and then he sits back, and lets go of it. “The bishop in New York said very much the same,” he observes, “at three times the length, into a microphone that kept failing. I took it as a sign. I am told that is the correct response to a sign.”

It’s a good argument. It’s Thomas with the Chesterton showing — nature bent toward its end, and grace doing the bending — and he has heard her make it about Flannery O’Connor, and about the Saints, and once about a cat. He knows which joint the knife goes in. What he hears is an argument, and he has an answer for it.

choices.text: “A hook is still a hook. Tell her that.”
response: “And the fish doesn’t get a vote,” Jack says, to Hale. “Waugh calls it grace because Waugh’s the one holding the rod.”
Hale relays it with relish. “Mr. Costigan is on the side of the fish.”
“Tell him the fish is drowning in air, Professor,” Lena says. “It just hasn’t noticed yet.”
Evan writes something in the margin of the roster. From the door end it looks very much like *fish*.

choices.text: “Tell Miss Broussard that Father Brown caught a jewel thief with that line. Waugh borrowed the tackle.”
response: “Plagiarism,” Hale says, purring. “Lovely. The chair adores a crime.” He gets up and writes PLAGIARISM on the whiteboard under the question, with a small, happy flourish, and sits down again.
“Tell Mr. Costigan the thief gave back the silver and went off a penitent,” Lena says, to Hale. “It’s the same story, Professor. That’s what the tackle is *for*.”
The library copy crackles; its owner has turned to the front to look for the Chesterton, and there isn’t any.

choices.text: “Tell her the thread’s the best thing in the book. It’s how Sebastian ends up at that gate.”
response: Hale relays it, and then, for the first time since he came in, says nothing clever after it.
“Yes,” Lena says, to Hale, quieter than she has been all afternoon.
“Good,” Hale says, after a while, to no one in particular, and looks displeased with himself for having said it.
Yusuf takes the cap off his pen, looks at the point, and puts the cap back on.

choices.text: “Tell Miss Broussard that renunciation’s easy when it’s somebody else’s love you’re giving up.”
choices.key: In Hale’s seminar, through the chair, you told Lena renunciation’s easy when it’s somebody else’s love you’re giving up. Hale relayed it.
response: The table goes quiet the way it went quiet last Wednesday, and Caleb’s stillness stops being a joke.

Hale could stop it. Last Wednesday he stood up and did. Today he folds his hands on the roster and turns his head the long way round and sends it down the varnish word for word, beautifully, in the voice he keeps for Housman, so that it arrives at the window end with nothing knocked off it.
Lena sets her pencil down beside the book, parallel to it. “Professor,” she says, very pleasantly, “please tell Mr. Costigan I’ll take that under advisement.”
Yusuf’s cap stays on his pen.

journal.title: Prof. Adrian Hale
journal.text: Wrote *The Consolations of Disbelief*. Wrote me a postcard. Walked into Hollis 302 at 1:07 with wine on his cuff and asked us to prove we have souls. Saw my face at the Anchor before he could put it to the nine pages. Called me a spaniel. Some nights he drinks alone in the Anchor’s back booth after midnight and says Housman to the window. Tips like he’s apologizing. Wrote his doctorate on moral luck. Asked me if the lucky one sleeps. Lent me his own copy of Williams’s *Moral Luck*, his Oxford pencil arguing with Williams in the margins on a first-name basis. Wants it back with mine in it. I owe him more than one. Gave me a pocket Housman for Danny, foxed, wartime. No margins. They’d only erase them. Has a deaf old greyhound named Bishop Berkeley. Brought him to the Blessing of the Animals to annoy Fr. Osei. Osei finished his limerick for him. Asked me if the Housman had gone. Says when you leave something, look at it. Newman did. Threw a dinner at the cliff end of Del Playa. Told a man asking Yusuf about Fort Hood that Yusuf’s a guest, not a spokesman. Read our margins out loud. Stopped in the middle of Lena’s, and folded it away. Told Caleb he doesn’t answer devotion. Collected our margins. Read Lena’s on mine: Neither do I. The final’s oral, December 16th — each of us defends the other’s best argument, and he’s the opponent. Told the room to keep Yusuf’s chair. The last seminar: Lena said nothing for an hour, and he told us to note the date. By Friday we each email him which of the other’s arguments we’ll defend. If we pick a weak one, he’ll know. Both picks came in. Not surprised, not disappointed — at his age the same thing as joy. Wednesday, two o’clock. Come as you are. The oral: she’d sent him Augustine. Lena first, then me. He knew which one I’d picked. I don’t yet know what I know, he said. He said it was an argument; he’s told they still occur. Marks posted on the solstice. I did well, which he’d like me to understand is not the same as being right. He and Berkeley are spending Christmas in Marisol. Spring: PHIL 109H, The Novel as Moral Argument, Mondays and Thursdays at one in Hollis 302. Opposite ends of the table, for the safety of the others. He got the baby in the king cake. ‘For the first quarter of an hour you were civil, and I didn’t care for it. I find I care for this even less.’ Carthage is not on the syllabus. The Conversion of St. Paul: he did Saul for Caleb. He’s in New York Thursday, being rude to a churchman on a stage, so Greene moved to his house Wednesday with the State of the Union on — phones in the dog’s bowl, bring a guest, sides assigned: me for Sarah’s silence, Lena against. Opposite ends of a door. He turned the President off before the rebuttal. When Lena and I went at each other across his table he stood up and stopped it, in a voice I’ve never heard out of him, and he wasn’t amused. Berkeley felt it through the floor. On the deck he said the table was his. He asked where a Catholic goes at eight on a Wednesday. Give him my regards. He blessed my dog. He may like to do it again. Monday’s seminar was cancelled. Gloria says he sat in the Anchor till close Sunday, reading her Housman. Thursday he made Lena and me speak only through him — all remarks to the chair. *Brideshead*: whether Julia’s right to send Charles away. He relayed every word. Lena’s gone two weeks, he says. I’ll have the table.

body: At ten to two the sun gets all the way through for the first time today and lies down the table from the window as far as the middle, where Hale is sitting, and he shuts his eyes in it like a cat on a sill.
“The chair,” he says, without opening them, “would like to hear about the end. The chair has always been partial to endings. They are the only part of a book a man can’t revise by talking.”

“The Epilogue, Professor,” Lena says. “It’s the war. Charles is a captain, nobody’s painter anymore, and the army has moved his company into Brideshead without telling him where they were going. The soldiers have done to the house what soldiers do. And the chapel’s been opened up again, for the troops, and in front of the altar there’s a little red lamp — an ugly one, Waugh makes very sure we know it’s ugly — and it’s burning again. Somebody lit it. Charles goes in and kneels, and says a prayer, an old one, that he’s only just learned.” Her hand is on the cover. “And Julia isn’t in it, Professor. Have y’all noticed that? She’s abroad with her sister, doing war work, and the book doesn’t even follow her. She did her part at her father’s bedside and the book let her go too. He kneels because Julia let him go. That’s the whole architecture. If she’d married him he’d be on a terrace in the south of France with a sketchbook and a grievance. Her no is what put him on his knees.”
Hale opens his eyes and relays it, all of it, down to *a grievance*. “Miss Broussard,” he adds, “offers the chair a terrace in the south of France, and declines it on Mr. Ryder’s behalf.”

The table holds still for it. The library copy has stopped crackling. Yusuf’s coffee is at his mouth and not going anywhere. In the sun the varnish shows every ring and scratch that thirty years of seminars have left in it, and at the window end the light has reached Lena’s book and the backs of her hands and stopped there, as if the sun had been told about the chair too.

It’s her best one. From the door end he can see the shape of it entire — the no as the hinge the book swings on, grace coming in by the wound — and he can see the place where it’s too neat, because it’s always too neat when she’s winning, and that’s where he goes in.
Jack has his answer in his mouth before Hale is through, and he waits for Hale to be through, because those are the rules, and they are the best rules anybody has made for him in a week.

choices.text: “He kneels because he’s grieving. Grief isn’t grace. Tell her.”
response: “Mr. Costigan says grief is not grace,” Hale tells the window, “and would like that minuted.”
“Tell him grief is the door grace uses, Professor,” Lena says. “It doesn’t knock at the front.”
Hale relays it and adds nothing, which is the most anybody has seen him add all hour. Caleb mouths *the front* to himself, approving, and stops when he catches Jack catching him.

response.text: Hale, closing the book: “Mr. Costigan has the text. Miss Broussard has the book.”
Hale, after a silence, to nobody: “I have never once seen two people agree so thoroughly in order to avoid looking at each other.”

Hale: “The chair is exhausted. The chair would like a drink.” Nobody laughs; Caleb tries.

response: “An army chaplain,” Jack says, to Hale. “A builder. Some private from Liverpool with a box of matches. People who never read the book. The lamp doesn’t care whose bargain it was.”

“I’ll paraphrase,” says Hale.

s14c.slug: THURSDAY · 2:15 PM · HOLLIS HALL, 302 — THE CARD
body: At a quarter past Hale shuts his book on one finger and stands, and gets his coat off the back of the chair. “Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace,” he tells the table, working an arm into a sleeve, apparently without hearing himself. “Miss Broussard will be absent for the next two weeks, attending to football and family.” He looks down the length of the table to the door end. “Mr. Costigan, you’ll have the table.”

Then the room is getting up. Caleb unfreezes all at once. At the door he stops beside Jack’s chair, and in the twang he keeps for Scripture says, low, “And the chair spake unto them, saying, Go ye through me,” and waits to be thanked for it, and isn’t, and stays in the doorway doing up his backpack one strap at a time. The girl with the library copy is negotiating it back into her bag past the plastic. Yusuf puts his cup in the bin by the door and the pen in his shirt pocket, and stands there a moment with his hand on the pocket. “Half-duplex,” he says, mostly to himself. “One direction at a time, through a relay. It works. It’s just slow.” At the window end Lena is putting things away in an order: the Waugh, the pencil, the legal pad.

The sun has gone back in, and the eucalyptus has started up again outside the glass. Evan unclips the roster and says to the room, “Thursday, then,” and to Jack, in the flattest Minnesota he has, “Table’s all yours, I guess,” and hears it as it comes out, and busies himself with the clip.
When Jack shifts on the chair he can feel the corner of the card through the paperback in his back pocket, a stiff place in Book Three.

choices.text: *Slide the card back down the table to her. Not a word.*
choices.key: Lena sent you a card asking you to New Orleans — you’d be welcome. After Hale’s, you slid it back down the table to her without a word.

journal.title: Lena Broussard
journal.text: New Orleans. Two seventeen. Classics. Hale paired us for the semester. Makes a roux like she’s taking a vow and expects you to keep up. Her father sells Gulf shrimp — Broussard’s Seafood, Banks Street. Boyfriend: Wes Arceneaux — Tulane, civil engineering, the boat at sixteen. Calls at 8:04 on the dot. Her grandmother, Lucille Guidry, died in the storm in ’05; they buried her in November, in the good dress. The medal came back to her mother in a plastic bag. She has never asked her mother one question. The year after, she went to Mass every morning to yell at God, and somewhere in there it stopped being a fight. Paints a mean fleur-de-lis. Said hi to Danny. Says she’s going to be defense. Walked her home the long way from Pi Lam: the beach, the creek, the tower, the Commons, the Lagoon bench. Wes calls from somewhere loud lately; her brother Luc is with him. She’s decided not to notice. The Tuesday of the wake he called on the dot, from his room. He came for Columbus Day weekend to see the Pacific. She’d told him it’s a threat. He touched it at two in the morning. Came to Marisol for the money, she says — Notre Dame gave her half. Went to Hale’s office to tell him he was wrong about who gets to forgive. Cried for Anders on the roof and didn’t give an inch. Stayed till the chimes. There’s a sentence she hasn’t finished. Her middle name is Thérèse; October first is her feast. She erased *Show Lena* out of the Hopkins herself, so Danny could have it. At midnight I gave her *Story of a Soul* with my margins in it, and she wouldn’t let me erase a word. On the beach she asked if I know what I’m doing. I don’t. She laughed. At the elevator: ‘That was a terrible thing to be glad about.’ Brought Wes to everything. Wouldn’t walk past the last house on Seacliff toward the Point; said she was cold. At the stove she gave Becca the spoon. Monday night, two floors down, on the phone to New Orleans: ‘He’s my friend, Wes.’ Plays the piano in the Delgado basement — the one nobody admits to playing. Two years at the Rosary. At five in the morning she played the Saints on the Ferrer carillon with her fists, one bell flat, and said it wasn’t flat, it was New Orleans. Wes told her what I said on the beach, and what I didn’t. On a motel porch above Lucia at three in the morning she told me I can’t say her name like that. She asked what I decided. Not to be the one who wrecks anything, I said. She said okay. Then: me neither. Bought her Mémère a fruitcake from the monks, in exact change. ‘A girl writes the thing she wants first, Youngstown.’ Halloween: Flannery O’Connor, with a stuffed peacock tagged 57. Andalusia. She wouldn’t go past the last house on Seacliff, not even for Laney. ‘I came as her. I never said she was right.’ In the last minute of the extra hour, she put my hat back on. s14d.slug: THURSDAY · 2:35 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE LOADING DOCK

body.text: He comes back from Hollis by the lagoon path with the *Brideshead* in his back pocket and nothing in it now but his place, and goes around the side of Delgado to the dock.
He comes out of the lobby with the brass click still in his ear and goes around the side of the building, past the bike racks, to the dock.
He comes out of the lobby and goes around the side to the dock, with his own two words somewhere in the wall behind him, in the dark of a brass box.
He comes around the side of Delgado to the dock with the book in his back pocket and the card still in it, keeping his place.

body: The loading dock is where Delgado keeps the part of itself it doesn’t show: two dumpsters, a tower of blue milk crates, a pallet of paper towels shrink-wrapped against the weather, the grease barrel with its lid chained on. Somebody from the kitchen takes breaks out here: there’s a milk crate turned over by the steel door for a seat, and beside it a Folgers can of sand bristling with butts, and the smell of the habit has got into the cinderblock. A gull stands on the dumpster lid with its head on one side, auditing the grease barrel. A dining-hall truck is idling at the foot of the ramp with its back doors open and nobody in it. There’s weather coming in off the water; he can taste the salt even back here, and the truck’s exhaust lies along the concrete and won’t rise.

It starts in his mouth, as it always does — a dry place at the back of the tongue, a taste first, before his hands know anything about it — and then his hands know. The pack is in the left pocket of the Carhartt with the lighter tucked into the cellophane, and his fingers have found it before he’s decided they could. In the right pocket is the tin. He carried it to Ohio and back over Christmas, and it has ridden in this coat ever since, and he hasn’t opened it.

choices.text: *Light one.*
choices.key: After Hale’s you smoked one on the Delgado loading dock.
response: One Marlboro out of the soft pack, lit in the lee of the grease barrel on the second try. He smokes it standing at the edge of the dock with the truck’s exhaust coming up around his shoes, and it tastes like nothing for three drags and then like the garage on Glenwood in February. Six drags and it’s done.
He grinds it out on the dock’s steel edge and drops the butt in the dumpster, because somebody from the kitchen sweeps this dock, and it won’t be him.

choices.text: *Put it back.*
response: He puts the pack back in the Carhartt and zips the pocket over it, and stands there with both hands in his pockets until the driver comes out of the kitchen door with a hand truck of empty crates, loads them, slams the back doors, and takes the truck away down the ramp and the smell with it.

choices.text: *Open the tin. Count them.*
response: The tin comes out of the right-hand pocket warm from him. The hinge is stiff from not being asked to do anything. He opens it on the dock rail, out of the wind.

Eleven. He counts them a second time with one finger, the way Nonna counts change at the Giant Eagle, because the first count is never the one you sign for. Eleven. He closes it and puts it back where it rides.

choices.text: *Count them again.*
response: Eleven. Still eleven. He closes it and puts it back where it rides.
